title: Find and Remove Hazards
subtitle: A first pass catches the dangers that are obvious the moment you finally look, and walks straight past the rest. This chapter makes Safety thorough: a calm, room-by-room hunt that carries the same short set of questions into every space, finds the hazards hiding in plain sight, and removes each one the moment it is found. Find it, and fix it now.

They do not need the safety lens or the triage re-taught (Chapter 20 did that); they need a repeatable, thorough method they can run themselves, room by room, to find and remove the hazards a first pass always misses, without turning the home into a place of constant dread. A home full of unnoticed hazards is the normal case, because adults habituate to their own space; the fix is a short set of questions carried room by room, not guilt or fear.
core_promise: Make your home thoroughly safe, room by room, today, without alarm. Learn why the obvious hazards are the few and the hidden ones the many (a first pass finds the dangers that are obvious the moment you look, a hunt finds the ones that never will be), and why familiarity is what hides them. Run a hazard hunt: a calm, systematic, room-by-room walk that carries the same five safety questions into every space and leaves nothing to memory. Carry the five plain questions, could someone fall, could something burn, could something poison or choke or strangle, could something fall or cut or crush, could water and electricity meet, and learn the family of hidden hazard each one surfaces. Recognize the camouflaged hazards a first pass walks past, the ordinary object doing a quiet second job. Remove each hazard the moment you find it, because a danger is only handled once it is gone, and when a full fix is bigger than now, make it safe now and schedule only the rest. Find it, and fix it now.

No fear-mongering, no graphic injury, no alarmist statistics, and no force or violence framing of the hunt, you hunt for hazards the way you hunt for your keys, and you remove them the way you remove a typo. The payoff is a home whose quiet dangers are simply gone. the_hunt_and_the_rule.the_hazard_hunt: The hero, less a gadget than a habit of moving through the house. Three things make it a hunt rather than another glance. It is systematic: you go room by room, in an order, so no space is skipped because you happened not to think of it. It is fixed: you carry the same short list of questions into every room, so the search does not depend on what you happen to remember to look for on a given day. And it ends in action: you fix what you find before you leave the room, so finding a hazard and removing it are one motion, not two. The method is almost aggressively boring, and that is the point; boring is what thorough looks like. The definition, frozen: a hazard hunt is a calm, systematic walk through the whole home, one room at a time, asking the same short set of safety questions in every space and removing each hazard you find before you move on; where a first pass catches what is obvious, the hunt is built to catch what is hidden. The method, frozen: go room by room, ask the same few questions in each, fix what you find before you leave. What the hunt is really designed to defeat is camouflage, frozen: the dangerous thing is rarely the ugly one, it is the ordinary object doing a second, quiet job you never gave it, the lamp cord that is also a tripwire, the old remote that is also a battery a small child can reach, the space heater that is also a flame a foot from the curtain. You are not hunting for junk or mess, which the earlier S's already cleared, but for ordinary, tidy, useful things doing a dangerous second job.
the_hunt_and_the_rule.the_five_questions: The short list you carry into every room, home-scaled from the questions the method has always asked on a safety walk and deliberately small enough to hold in your head. In every room, ask (frozen set): could someone fall here; could something here burn, or catch fire; could something here poison, choke, or strangle; could something here fall, cut, or crush; could water and electricity meet. Between them they catch the great majority of what hurts people at home, and each is a different lens finding a different family of hidden hazard. Could someone fall looks down and at the edges: the sliding rug, the tread with a stray shoe, the wet patch by the tub, the top of the stairs. Could something burn looks for heat too near things that burn and electricity asked to do too much: the heater a foot from the curtain, the candle under the shelf, the overloaded outlet, the dryer lint. Could something poison, choke, or strangle looks low and for the small and the looped: the chemicals and medicines within reach, the button batteries and coins and small parts, the looped blind or curtain cord at a child's height. Could something fall, cut, or crush looks up and at what is heavy and free: the unanchored tall bookcase or dresser, the heavy box up high, the knives at the counter's edge. Could water and electricity meet looks in the wet rooms: the hairdryer near the filled basin, the frayed cord by the sink. You do not need to memorize categories or become an inspector; you need five plain questions and the willingness to ask all five in every room.
the_hunt_and_the_rule.find_it_and_fix_it_now: The rule, and the temptation to resist: to do the finding now and the fixing later, walking the whole home with a notepad. Resist it, because that is the one move that quietly turns a hazard hunt back into a hazard museum. The found-not-fixed reframe, frozen: a hazard you have found but not fixed is not handled, it is scheduled, and a hazard on a schedule is still a hazard, still able to hurt someone on any ordinary day before its turn comes up, and the only safe place for a danger is gone. A written-down hazard is exactly as dangerous as an un-written-down one; the child does not know the button battery is on your list, the fire does not check whether you meant to move the heater this weekend. So you close the gap to nothing and fix each hazard the moment you find it. This is the source's oldest safety instruction, address all possible safety issues immediately, home-scaled, and the whole reason the hunt ends in action rather than in a list. Carry a roll of grip tape, a few cabinet latches, and an empty box, not a notepad. Most home hazards are cheap and quick to remove, and the fix is usually smaller than the worry was. The honest exception: now and then a full fix is genuinely bigger than now, and the rule still holds with a small amendment, make it safe now, even if you cannot make it finished now; reduce the danger to near nothing immediately, and schedule only the part that truly cannot be done on the spot. What you never do is walk away from a live hazard having changed nothing but your to-do list.

worked_example.applied_pass: Let me walk it with you, room by room. Start in the kitchen, because it holds more of all five kinds of hazard than any other room: a slick spot where the dishwasher leaks worth a look, a pot handle turned out over the front edge turned in (a two-second fix you will now do by reflex forever), a butane lighter in an open drawer at child height moved up high, the knives pushed to the very edge of the counter slid back. The bathroom is quick and high-value: the hairdryer unplugged and moved to a drawer away from the water, the gripless bath mat given a grip pad, a nightlight in because most bathroom falls happen in the dark. The living room is where camouflage lives: the tall bookcase that has stood free of the wall for years gets a simple anti-tip strap today, the old remote whose battery cover has gone loose gets a strip of tape until you replace it, and the lamp cord Chapter 20 promised would take a real hunt comes out from under the rug, where it was both a thing to trip on and a wire being slowly crushed and heated, and is routed along the wall. The stairs and hall want two of the questions: the curled hall runner tacked flat, a nightlight at the top of the stairs. The child's room wants the poison-choke-strangle question most: the blind cord that hangs in a loop at exactly a toddler's height wound up onto a cleat out of reach, the small parts and coins on the low shelf moved up. And the launch pad, paying off the last of Chapter 20's teasers: the little space heater that sits a foot from the curtain moved to a clear spot with a rule about the curtain, the charging cords tucked so no foot catches them. Nothing needed a deep clean or a rearrange; it was already sorted and arranged and clean. It just, in a handful of small ways, could have hurt someone, and now, room by room, it cannot.
worked_example.tally: You carried five plain questions through the whole home, one room at a time, and removed what they found before you left each room. That is the fourth S made thorough: not a first pass on the obvious dangers, but a complete sweep that reached the hidden ones, the button battery and the blind cord and the unanchored bookcase and the heater by the curtain, the hazards that would have survived any number of glances because they were wearing the disguise of ordinary things. Because a whole-home hunt removes a roomful of hidden hazards, far more than a first pass, the friction meter TAKES A SECOND Safety step off the Shine-complete milestone toward the goal. Again nothing got cleaner or tidier and no object found a better home; the daily friction is exactly what it was this morning. What dropped, again, is the home's exposure to harm, the deepest kind of friction there is, the friction of the worst day, the one you are keeping from ever arriving. The step is a touch larger than the first, because a thorough hunt clears more than a first glance did, and still, in absolute terms, a measured one, because the earlier S's already cleared the bulk of what this meter tracks and safety moves it in the smaller, quieter increments of things locked down rather than swept out. Chapter 20's first-Safety-step position is now the dashed ghost just behind the live needle; Chapter 19's Shine-complete milestone sits further back as a passed marker; the GOAL crosshair, tagged purpose, stays ahead on the green calm side, because Safety is finished only when the home is made to keep itself safe, which is Chapter 22, and Standardize and Sustain follow. This is a STEP, not a milestone.
